source.title: Advancing Zero-shot Text-to-Speech Intelligibility across Diverse Domains via Preference Alignment
source.authors: Xueyao Zhang; Yuan-Cheng Wang; Chaoren Wang; Zi-Niu Li; Zhuo Chen; Zhi-Zheng Wu

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper explicitly tests whether preference data made with less capable TTS systems can improve more capable systems, but it uses DPO on preference pairs and reports WER rather than the original PGR measure.
record.gate_note: Table 4 reports before/after INTP-alignment WER for CosyVoice 2 and Ints, which were not used to construct INTP, alongside the INTP-generating models. The paper does not calculate PGR. Table 5's data-composition and negative-sample ablations do not compare strong students with their weak supervisors, so they are not recorded as V2 results. Figure 2's flattened subjective reading-accuracy values are not assigned to individual models here.
record.test_reason: The paper borrows the 'weak-to-strong' label (P3, citing Burns et al.) but does not test the claim. First, the supervision is not the weaker models' labels. Preference pairs are ranked by external ASR WER (Whisper-large-v3, Paraformer-zh) and by human-guided perturbations. The weaker models (ARS, F5-TTS, MaskGCT) only generate candidate audio. Second, there is no strong ceiling and no PGR. Third, CosyVoice 2 and Ints already beat the data-generating models on average WER before any training (13.09 and 11.97 vs MaskGCT 14.04), so 'student beats supervisor' is not produced by the training. What is measured is a different construct: transfer of a preference dataset built from other, weaker generators' outputs to stronger generators. This is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors say INTP, though built from weaker models, works for stronger CosyVoice 2 and Ints, and call this 'weak-to-strong generalization'. They also report WER and N-CMOS gains for all five models. Iterative alignment on Ints gives further but smaller second-round gains, which they attribute to base-model capacity.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains TTS systems with DPO on preference pairs, including comparisons across models and human-guided perturbed negatives; it reports WER rather than the original PGR. INTP is not exclusively labels from a single weaker supervisor.
record.method_sensitivity: WER outcomes vary across evaluation domains and models; the reported improvement is not uniform in magnitude.

fits_no_version.finding: DPO on INTP preference pairs reduces WER for CosyVoice 2 (13.09 to 10.56 avg) and Ints (11.97 to 7.96 avg). INTP pairs are generated by weaker TTS models and ranked by ASR WER plus perturbations. Neither model was used to build the dataset. Gains hold in all four domains (Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preference data built from weaker generators' outputs, ranked by an external metric, improves stronger generators of the same task (dataset transfer to stronger models).

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The relevant WER results have no reported uncertainty estimates. The study does not calculate PGR, and its preference data includes multiple TTS systems and human-guided perturbations rather than a single weak supervisor's labels.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from the selected Table 4 WER results for the two models identified as the weak-to-strong students. Other Table 4 metrics (SIM and N-CMOS) do not measure intelligibility; Table 5 ablations and Table 6 iterative-alignment results do not test weak-to-strong performance against the weak supervisor.

untested.parts: No weak-supervisor labels, no strong ceiling, no PGR. The strong models already outperform the data generators before training.
No auxiliary confidence loss, supervisor ensembling or loss variants compared on PGR. Table 5 ablations are on ARS, a data-generating model.
No PGR as a function of supervisor/student size or task.
No exploitation, distribution-shift PGR or error-similarity analysis.
No vision. The speech setting is not a test of the weak-label effect.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's verdicts (supports/limits_scope on V1, V3) are withdrawn. The study's use of 'weak-to-strong' is nominal. Preference labels come from ASR WER and human-guided perturbation, not from weak models' judgments. The 'strong' students were already better than the generators before training. No PGR or ceiling is defined. The study is peer reviewed (ACL) and its code is released.

versions.untested_parts: PGR is not calculated. The preference dataset combines outputs from multiple TTS models with human-guided perturbed samples, rather than consisting solely of labels from one weak supervisor.
No comparison tests whether auxiliary confidence loss, supervisor ensembling, or loss variants raise PGR over naive fine-tuning.
The study varies TTS model and evaluation domain, but does not systematically vary supervisor/student size or test what representations predict PGR.
It does not test weak-to-strong PGR under distribution shift or whether gains shrink when weak and strong models make similar errors.
No theoretical conditions for beating a supervisor are tested.
